questions.q: In T-SQL, what happens to 'FirstName + MiddleName + LastName' when MiddleName is NULL?
options: MiddleName is treated as an empty string and the rest concatenates normally
Only MiddleName is dropped from the output column list
questions.explain: T-SQL's + operator propagates NULL — if any operand is NULL, the whole concatenated result is NULL.

questions.q: What does 'first_name + last_name' actually compute on MySQL?
options: Arithmetic addition (or an error/garbage result), because + is not a concatenation operator in MySQL
A syntax error that MySQL refuses to parse
questions.explain: MySQL's + is strictly arithmetic. There is no string-concatenation + in MySQL at all — CONCAT() is required.

questions.q: Which operator is the ANSI SQL standard's concatenation operator, used natively by Oracle and PostgreSQL?
questions.explain: || is the ANSI-standard concatenation operator, supported natively by Oracle and PostgreSQL (and standard SQL in general).

questions.q: What function is available on ALL FOUR dialects (SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL) as a concatenation option?
questions.explain: CONCAT() is supported across all four platforms, and it's the only concatenation mechanism MySQL offers at all (since + is arithmetic there).

questions.q: Why would a T-SQL developer's muscle memory with + be dangerous when first writing MySQL queries?
options: Because + silently performs arithmetic addition on MySQL instead of concatenating strings, often producing 0 or a coercion error instead of the expected joined string
Because + is forbidden syntax in MySQL and always throws an error
Because + concatenates correctly in MySQL too, so there's no real risk
Because MySQL requires semicolons after every +
questions.explain: MySQL treats + as pure arithmetic. Using it expecting concatenation (as in T-SQL) produces numeric coercion behavior, not the intended string result.
